newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Siberian farms see full fields but wary of selling.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Siberian farms see full fields but wary of selling.

text.p: Moscow is hoping Siberia's grain harvest will help offset shortages in other parts of the country, but local agricultural officials worry about heavy rains and say they may keep any extra wheat.

"Folk have been calling from Moscow and bidding higher prices -- but traders don't want to pay up front," said Vladimir Krivtsov, a crops specialist at the regional agriculture department in the southern central Siberian city of Novosibirsk.
"Nobody wants to work with Moscow."
Farmers across Russia in places like Yarki, a rural village just outside Novosibirsk, can now largely sell their wheat as they wish as the sector tries to embrace market economy reforms.
But their main buyer, the state, is a notoriously late and stingy payer, while private traders are usually able to fork out enough cash only for small purchases at a time.
That means peasants distrust the government as a customer -- but that they are also unsure about selling to private traders.

The Russian government is still active, through semi-private regional buying agencies left over from the Soviet era, in procuring grain from regions like Novosibirsk for the army, the Arctic and big cities.

The Novosibirsk Food Corporation, a government agency which buys for regional needs, says it may buy Siberian wheat for its parent organisation, the Federal Food Corporation -- but it is unclear how the organisation will pay for it.

"(Deputy Prime Minister Alexander) Zaveryukha has agreed to Federal Food Corporation purchases, but whether the money will appear is unclear," said Svetlana Lipatova, the Novorsibirsk Food Corporation's deputy director.
Local officials and grain experts say Siberian regions like Novosibirsk and neighbouring Altai and Omsk may have 2.0-2.5 million tonnes of wheat for sale to other parts of Russia.

Local grain specialists say western Siberia, whose harvest is well under way, could reap as much as 13 million tonnes of grain this year, far above last year's 11.2 million and above the 1991-1995 average of 10.7 million tonnes.
But in the wet Siberian fields, Viktor Mustafin, a crop specialist at Yarovkoe, a privatised farm outside Novosibirsk, said that a rainy summer could hurt quality and yields.
Independent agricultural consultancy SovEcon Ltd last month revised down its western Siberian grain forecast to 9.3 million tonnes from 10.5 million, citing low yields.
Zaveryukha said this month that rains in Siberia had been torrential and that Russia's total harvest would depend on how Siberian crops fare.
He hoped a good Siberian crop would make up for shortfalls of high-quality milling wheat in big Russian cities and in other areas where the harvest has not fared as well.
But Siberian grain sources are less sure the grain will travel.
"Small-time traders pay more and in up front cash, but they buy only 40 to 50 tonnes at a time," Mustafin said.
Mikhail Golovatyuk, head of the agricultural economics department of the Siberian Scientific Research Institute outside Novosibirsk, said farmers' biggest problem is not growing wheat.
"Over the last two years selling -- not growing -- has been the difficult task," he said.
The cash-strapped state is still a late payer -- some Novosibirsk farmers said they were paid for 1995 output only this spring, and often in goods like diesel and fertiliser.
New, post-Soviet problems include soaring freight and rail costs, which make moving grain across the vast Russian landscape a costly endeavour.
"It is not profitable to ship grain from Siberia because of the high rail tariffs," Golovatyuk said.
"If freight and rail prices remain high, the amount of grain sent outside the region will be very low."

Vladimir Tyazhelnikov, deputy director of semi-private Novosibirskkhleboprodukt, a grain buying agency, said tariffs on a recent shipment of local oats to the Far East cost as much as the oats themselves.
It is tough to make ends meet in the southern Siberian steppe, where agricultural life is hard and market economy reforms creak slowly forward.
Still, officials said the Novosibirsk area has high grain reserves -- unlike much of the rest of the country, which ate its stocks after 1995's disastrous 63.4 million tonne harvest.
"Novosibirsk region had two million tonnes of 1995 grain in its reserves at the beginning of 1996," Golovatyuk said. "This year, it will store three million in reserves beyond its needs."
Still, some Siberian grain will be traded.
Tyazhelnikov said small shipments of flour have already been sent to Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan.

But Golovatyuk said much wheat could stay in the hands of farmers, whom he said would rather feed excess grain to cattle and then slaughter them to sell locally for quick cash than take a chance on selling grain directly to late-paying Moscow or unknown traders.
"These small farmers work on shoe-string margins and do not calculate the value of their labour," Golovatyuk said.
"They just need cash."
